title: A Dark and Heavy History
text:
The castle is very well preserved.  The guide that we had was a master story teller who told the history of Elmina with a lot of passion.  His understanding of the history was in depth and he also provided great commentary.  To allow us to experience a fraction of what the slaves experienced, we were placed in some of the dungeons with the doors closed.  
There are a couple of great shops where you can buy books and dvds about the history of the castle.  In addition you can purchase some Ghanian souvenirs.
The view over the town of Elmina is fantastic.

title: Heartbreaking but a necessary visit
text: The castle's history is simply unfathomable. The tour guide we had was passionate and knowledgeable.

title: Another ghastly reminder of human exploitation
text:
This castle is about 11kms from the Cape Coast Castle.

It has lot of similarities with Cape Coast Castle- the white walls, the horro stories within & the disgusting history of both the castles.

It is a historical structure that holds the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade that many countries try to disown & push under the carpet.. A spine chilling journey through dungeons where 150 humans were chained together & made to live a life which was wort then hell. The terrible treatment of humans for the quest for wealth via the Portuguese, Dutch &, English,held in varying times of Elmina Castle. A must see and experience and the preservation of this repulsive thing that was slavery!

Inside and out, Elmina Castle is a very imposing edifice indeed.  Its main claim to fame is that it's the oldest building in sub-Saharan Africa. It was established by the Portuguese in 1482 although most of what we see today is Dutch, post 1637. The British took over the Castle in 1872 and held it until Ghanaian independence in 1957. Subsequent restoration has been done by the Ghanaian government. Visitors are directed to an important building in the main courtyard, now a museum which tells the entire history of the area. It's in a former Portuguese church (1596), which was turned by the Dutch into a market. The Portuguese, Dutch and Brits were all involved in the slave trade and the first port of call on the guided tour is the slave dungeons. Hundreds at any one time were incarcerated here before being led down a tunnel to the "door of no return", a narrow slot, which at one time gave on to the sea, which has since receded. Boats then carried the slaves to ships, which took the captives direct to the Americas. We were also shown a gallery, from where the Governor chose female slaves, who were then taken to the Governor's substantial quarters. It's likely that the women who subsequently gave birth were released. Similar stories are told at other Ghanaian landmarks, e.g. the Cape Coast Castle and the James Fort Prison, Accra. 

Definitely one visit

title: Elmina Castle Visit
text:
A great experience, the impact of the trans Atlantic slave trade will stay with me for a long time. May we vow never ever again to allow such slavery. The walk that slaves had to take and the door of no return
Is etched in my heart forever.

title: A visual portrait, of the African horror story.
text: The Elmina dungeons is the location where the captured and enslaved African people were warehoused and tortured until they were shipped around the world, to slave farms. There are guides on the site that give a detailed history and accounting, of the salved trade. The dungeons have been kept, in tact so that you get a clear and precise undertaking, of what transpired during that era, in time. If you have an ounce of humanity, you must mentally prepare yourself, for some, of the worst atrocities that happened, to people.

title: Inspiring
text: We took hotel car and driver to see it.  You can easily get there and back in a day trip.  I read "Things Fall Apart" on flight over to Ghana which is a wonderful book and helped put things in perspective.  It's hot to walk around and very sunny and we brought sun hats and umbrella for shade.  It's not a castle it's a dungeon, not sure why it's called that.  Scene of horrible atrocities.  Tour was worth it not expensive.  Guide spoke well and with great conviction.

title: Worth visiting

title: Walk in the past
text: We wanted to visit the castles but to be honest it was very depressing.  It was rich in history and full of information.  Visiting the castle and hearing the stories behind it reminds you how humans can be so mean and horrible to one another.  This should never have happened, treating each other like commodities.

title: A smaller version of the Cape Coast Castle, but tells a poignant story of the slave trade
text: The Elmina Castle tells a sad tale about the history of the African people. Slavery played quite a role in the history of Africa and indeed, the bookshop in the Castle offers some insight in the form of books and CD on the history of the slave trade. Our tour guide was amazing and it was really interesting to also see the role played by Christianity in the Slave trade. The Church was right next to the dungeons, a similar scenario that also plays out when we see the stark contrast between the cell where the condemned slave was kept and the next door cell for unruly soldiers.We leave Elmina with the commitment that never again shall humanity witness the level of brutality that was witnessed and perpetrated during the slave trade era.

title: So much history, so little time
text:
The castle has been standing since the 1400s, having served not only as a trading site but also as a slave trading site. 
There's so much history that the guide can't possibly do it all justice. In hindsight, I would recommend to do some reading pre-visit.
What it does, successfully, in a short period of time, is give the visitor a grasp of the unimaginable conditions in which the kidnapped, captive Africans were kept.

title: Slave dungeon
text: There is nothing about this place that should be call a castle. This place should have a proper name of being called a Slave Torture dungeon.

title: Moving
text: Elmina castle is a story of brutal white colonialism.  To walk through the dungeons and learn how these poor people were treated is humbling.  The door of no return is something you need to experience. The cell where they left unruly slave to starve to death, the womens dungeon where the governor would pick women to rape.... horrific. But what is really disgusting and never ever mentioned is the fact that it was Africans selling Africans into slavery.

title: Er dette virkelig et slavehus?
text: Etter å ha besøkt store slavefort i f.eks. Ghana, så ble dette huset litt merkelig. Slavehuset på Goree er langt under en tiendedel av størrelsen av de i Ghana, og spor etter de slavene som ble holdt der fant ikke jeg ihvertfall. Når det er sagt, så er det jo en fryktelig historie som må fortelles, og sånn sett kanskje dette huset gjør nytten sin? Jeg fikk imidlertid ikke så mye ut av besøket i dette huset.

title: Émouvant
text: Cette petite île est aujourd'hui bien paisible, elle est certes très visitée mais elle a su garder un certain charme.La maison des esclaves est une visite incontournable quand on va au Sénégal pou comprendre l'évolution de ce pays. Le responsable du site évoque avec des mots simples, ordinaires toute l'horreur de ces lieux: les conditions de vie inhumaines, la séparation des familles  sur des continents différents, l"engraissage" des personnes pour atteindre le poids de vente, et la porte sans retour.  C'est vraiment émouvant.

title: A futura memoria
text: Sono tornato una seconda volta sull'isola di Goree perché già la prima volta, alcuni mesi fa, mi aveva lasciato una forte emozione la traccia storica di questa isola, punto di concentramento e poi di deportazione di milioni di africani destinati a finire la loro misera vita come schiavi nel Nuovo Mondo. La Casa degli schiavi, dove per casa si deve intendere una struttura simile ad un carcere con camere anguste e malsane in cui venivano rinchiusi in catene uomini, donne e bambini. Guardare da vicino quelle celle, i ceppi di ferro, le catene e i collari di ferro, significa percepire la sofferenza di questa gente e comprendere di quanta malvagità e violenza i bianchi erano dotati. In luogo che fa riflettere e che a me che sono un bianco mi ha fatto vergognare di esserlo. Possiamo solo avere tanta compassione per chi ha sofferto e chiedere scusa a nome dei nostri simili francesi, inglesi, olandesi e portoghesi che si sono macchiati di tale vergogna.

title: African Drumming - yeyy!!!!
text:
We spent a day in Cape coast and knew exactly what we signed in for when we visited the slave castle (a must for every human!). So we started there and then booked ourselves for a portion of joy in the afternoon, something completly different - African Drumming workshop. 
It was wonderful, so, wonderful! All the reviews I read here before referred to the cooking classes and the Batic work, but once I realized this little center offers also drumming, all other options were of the table. We booked a day in advance, by phone and showed up at the tiny shop, which is the hub of this great initiative. You should stop there and admire the wonderful selection of the ladies' crafts and buy some - it's fair trade (I did). Any way, we were taken to a nearby large yard, where 2 guys waited with African drums. The instructor showed us different moves, patiently yet enthusiastically, demonstrating and correcting and sure enough, after a while we were able to drum some beats with him and his friend. It was very warm, outside, not far from the beach, but we were so happy (especially after spending the whole morning in the dungeons). As we were drumming, everybody started singing, what a great party! When we thought the lesson was over, another girl appeared, and taught us also some African dance moves, which we happily followed. All in all - this was a wonderful, wonderful afternoon - if music is your passion, do yourselves a favor and book  this workshop!

Mit dem mobilen Holzkohlegrill dann das Kochen in mehreren Etappen: Die Yamsscheiben gekocht, die Kochbananen frittiert, die Bohnen und die Palawan-Sauce mit afrikanischem Spinat zubereitet.
Das alles immer unter fachkundiger und freundlicher Unterstützung von Esi.

Das Red Red mit gekochtem Yams und Palawan-Sauce schmeckte auch den Kinder sehr gut und sie wollen es zu Hause nachkochen.

Danke Esi für zwei schöne Stunden mit leckerem, selbstgekochtem ghanaischen Essen!
Sehr zu empfehlen!

title: Tribute to Freedom, Unity, and Founding Father in Ghana
text:
Our group of 17 received a guided tour of this memorial with Gardens, Mausoleum, Museum, and Statue that honors the activist who worked for Ghana independence.  this memorial sits on the former British polo grounds where independence was declared in 1957. Kwame Nkrumah served as president from 1957 to 1966 and this memorial was dedicated in 1992.  The structures are made of marble and topped with black star, the symbol of unity in Ghana.
The Italian marble mausoleum houses the remains of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah as well as those of his wife  Fathia.  The statue shows his headless body with a separate display for his head, which was found apart from this body.
The gardens provide an area of green, refreshing water, and symbol of hope.
Accessible restrooms. Accessible parking.

title: Words of Wisdom
text:
The Dr. Kwame Nkrumah Mausoleum and Memorial Park in Accra honors Ghana's first President, Kwame Nkrumah. The museum displays his belongings, documents, and photographs, providing insights into his life and Pan-Africanist ideals. I had a chance to visit this park in December 2024. During my visit, I was particularly moved by the inspiring quotes adorning the walls. These words, spoken by Nkrumah himself, continue to resonate, offering profound insights into his philosophy and aspirations. Some of his most famous quotes include:
1.	"I am not African because I was born in Africa but because Africa was born in me." 
2.	“We face neither East nor West: we face forward." 
3.	"The independence of Ghana is meaningless unless it is linked-up with the total liberation of the African Continent" 
4.	"We have awakened. We will not sleep anymore. Today, from now on, there is a new African in the world!" 
5.	"The best way of learning to be an independent sovereign state is to be an independent sovereign state."
6.	"The forces that unite us are intrinsic and greater than the superimposed influences that keep us apart."

title: A walk down memory lane
text:
The historically nostalgic edifice that takes you back in time and recounts the story of how slaves were treated and shipped abroad. This monstrous structure set at a strategically ideal location along the Central regional coastline with easy access to the Western region initially named São Jorge da Mina by the Portuguese, the Elmina castle as we now know it will go on to be declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1979.

It currently stands as the oldest European building in existence South of the Sahara, and a guided tour through its dungeons and dining area, corridors and chapel, residencies and occupancies makes you better appreciate the mix of emotions, intrigue, suspense, surprise, marvel and mysteries this historical treasure has to offer. 

Our onboard photographer made sure we captured all the memorable moments experienced on the trip.

title: history

title: The Door of No Return
text:
I took a three hour ride from Accra to Elmina Castle which is situated at the edge of a rough Atlantic Ocean. Stepping through the gate of the castle was reliving the days of slavery and the slave trade. It can make one get real emotional. It is a good place to take history students so they can see history come alive. The 'door of no return' stood out in my memory so much! It was the little slit in the wall through which slaves were pushed into waiting boats which took them to bigger ships which then took them to other lands. 
I left their with my name written on a shell, welcoming me to the area and to Ghana. There are young people at the gates of the castle who in  friendly manner introduce themselves and ask your name. They get the correct spelling then tell you that you will get a gift at the end of your visit into the castle. When you return to the outside you are given the shell and you are asked for a contribution. I saw a tourist arguing with one youngster as he wanted U$5 for the shell. (The shell did not value that.) It is best to change your money to cedis. 1USD- 5cedis.

title: Historical site to be seen

title: As good as in Cape Coast!
text: Elmina castle is the oldest European fortification built by Portuguese in 1482! The Dutch seized the fort from the Portuguese in 1637. The Dutch were busy with slave trade till 1814. They managed to sell the fort to British in 1872. The Brits did not use the Castle as a slave trade Fort and instead were recruiting the black soldiers for the war in Burma (Myanmar). The fee is 40 cedis for non-Ghanian nationalities and 30 for students. The tour is free of charge.

title: Why are human beeing so cruel to each other??
text: Seeing the depth of thinking that was built into the facility to deconstruct and humiliate a human being was humbling.  The experience was gut-wrenching and visceral.  Everyone should visit this people export facility, to understand how a human being was deconstructed, humiliated and then exported like a commodity or life-stock to then be labeled a slave and further humiliated until death.  Elmina should never be allowed to decay or effaced from the collective heritage of the world.

title: Accra City Tour 🇬🇭

title: Iconic and interesting
text:
I’m glad I went here and saw the memorial park and museum. It taught me more about the history of Ghana and the struggle to independence. However, the museum is sadly not very well maintained and the memorial itself looks like it is probably not up to its former glory. You can imagine what it must once have looked like with the fountains but now it’s a little run down. There were very very few tourists there when I visited, just me and another group, so I can understand that it would be hard to maintain it very well with so few tourists. It did feel like a very peaceful place and I am glad I went. It’s definitely an iconic place to visit in Accra. 

There are quite a few people trying to sell things just outside the gate so if you’re walking to and from the park like I was expect to be accompanied by men trying to convince you to buy things or to walk with them to their shops.

title: Historical feature that needs maintenance
text:
This place is so informative. However the maintenance is a big let down. The water feature and the gardens need to be put back into operation. 

The saddest part is the glass case containing the Cadillac that JFK gifted to Kwame Nkrumah. 

This vehicle would now not look out of place in your average junkyard. 

It is listing to one side and covered in dust. There's also no written commentary telling its story. 

The small museum towards the rear was great and gives a fantastic insight into Kwame Nkrumah and the journey of Ghana into independence.

title: Afternoon at Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park
text: Prior to my travel to Ghana, I had searched online for places to visit in Accra. The memorial park was one of the list toppers on the results I got. From the pictures I had seen the beautiful fountains and I was really looking forward to finding the same. Only to get there and see that the place is no longer as it is in the pictures online. I don’t think it still gets as many visitors as before therefore it is no longer as visually appealing as before. The place is rich in Nkrumah’s history though. I learnt so much and it was great to see quite a lot of Nkrumah’s belongings from the time he was in college till the time of his death.

title: Movind museum
text: The small museum is very interesting though there is not much written information. But you get interesting books in the gift shop. The whole park is somehow neglected, the fountains don't work as the usually don't do in Ghana.Kwame Nkrumahs life story is moving and once again the bloody CIA was behind the military coup with which he was ousted in 1966.

title: My Experience
text: A museum surrounded by a wide and large green park with statues and fountains.  Place to learn of Nkrumah's life & legacy.

title: Very Educational
text: The tour guide was great!! I highly  recommend a visit. The water feature was under construction when I visted.

title: Solemn Disregarded Pan African Ambitions
text: Pretty tired and unkempt park reflecting diminished regard for Nkruma an other Pan Africanists over the past 50 years. Nonetheless the park is a solemn place for reflection of those original ambitions and Hope's- particularly the photos in the museum and the lonely grave.

title: Where is water?
text: Enough people left their reviews here, so whatever I say, I can probably only repeat what someone else must’ve already said before. The only thing I may point out is the fact that I first visited this park in 2011. This year was my second visit. Back then, the fountains were working and the basin was full of water. This year, they were out of function and the basin was dry. If it was merely a temporary maintenance, then it’s fine. However, in Africa one can never know. It would be sad if it was a case of a more permanent neglect. When there is water, entire memorial looks much better.

title: Lovely!! You wont be Disappointed

title: Interesting Short Stop

Nice grounds/park  to wonder outside as well. Not much of a gift shop, but be careful of the vendors standing outside. They'll take your name and create souvenirs for your with your name on them, trying to guilt you into buying them.

title: Tour
text: It is one of the exciting attractions to visit in Ghana, it gives you the history of our first President. With all the beautiful fountain, Dignitaries gardens, the statues.

title: Poor organization for a national museum
text:
This location is open all week long and it’s easy to get in. However there is no one to welcome you when you walk in and there are no guides. You may walk by a gentleman or two as you walk through the place but they offer absolutely no help. I have heard that lighter skinned people and blacks with English/ American accents are treated differently but I haven’t confirmed this for myself. 

My initial visit was with an organized school group 16 years ago and it was the only time I experienced a guide there, perhaps because arrangements were made or there was better service at the time. The experience from my last two visits which were about 5 years apart is what I have recounted here. Friends and family have had similar experiences. 

As a museum designated to the first president of Ghana who is such an iconic figure, the organization at this place certainly needs to step up.

title: Worth the trip
text: Very interesting, important history, with knowledgeable guides, this memorial park is more of a small museum than a park. Plan two hours. Learn and understand. It’s quite moving when one learns about the bravery and resourcefulness of pan-African leadership in the middle of last century. Onward and upward.... always forward.

title: Kwame Nkrumah park

title: Old and still fine.
text:
After a couple of years since my last visit, I went with a friend to see the Museum this week. 
Not much of an improvement in the artefacts and art on display in the Museum since my last visit, but I was pleased that they had so many people visiting that day, and a couple of guided tours were underway.

Tickets were N200 (about 50cents) for adults, and N100 ($0.25) for children.

Opens every day 9am and closes 3pm on most days.

Points for:
-Nice for a short visit. So, even if you have a busy schedule, you can pop in. We spent about 30 minutes in all, to have a quick look at all the galleries. 

-Centrally located in Onikan, Lagos Island. It is adjacent to Ikoyi and close to Victoria Island. It is easily accessible, especially if you know the roads around the area.

-Free parking in large car park. 

-Nice grounds with trees. Nice place to have a picnic with family/friends.

-Nice museum shop, though dimly lit.

Points against:
-The air conditioning was off is the largest gallery. They said "currently under repairs"

-There's room for improvement in the display and labelling of items, as well as in other aspects of the Museum.

-Photos not allowed in galleries. Why?

title: An Unusual Museum
text: I always like to visit museums. This one was also a memorable experience, mostly because it is not a national museum you would expect. The building is quite old and there is no air conditioning, but the employees are trying very hard to make the whole experience nice. The entrance fee is 200 Nairas for Nigerians and 300 for tourists, plus the tour guide will ask you for some money in the end, but you tip him as much as you want (I gave him 1000 Nairas because my Nigerian friend told me that was enough). The museum currently hosts two exhibitions - one about Nigerian culture and the other one about the country's governments over the last couple of decades, and both are worth seeing.

title: Pass
text: Needs a refurbishment.  Not much here.  Hot.  Not very well kept displays.  Can finish in 20 minutes or so.

title: ummmm, only ok.
text: I visited Sunday on a Saturday, I was the only visitor. Entrance fee for foreigners: 300 naira (less than one Euro). The staff little interested, in my opinion, in explaining the history of the country, although the enm exhibition itself is beautiful.

title: Decent
text: I enjoyed my time there but wish there was more information and exhibits to see. What they have is informative and you do get a good insight on different cultures.

title: good but could be so much better
text: what there is is fine but more information about each exhibit would be nice, the political history section is done well, and the rest should follow suit. If you dont know Nigerian geography it is hard to put the exhibits into context.

title: Not so much artifacts, just good information
text: I was in some museums and I read only few lines of information because the collection itself is indeed the story and history. Here, you have to do a lot of reading, not so much visual arts collection. Though I love the information about their face marks. Nice facts, so cultural. I just hate the history of slavery..It will break your heart.

title: Great art work without being pampered through beautiful galleries!
text: Yes, this is not the British, Metropolitan or Gulbenkian museums.  Nonetheless, this Nigerian museum contains some stunning works of African wood and bronze artwork that you will never experience anywhere else and that will remind you where Picasso's source Cubist  inspiration came from! (Let's not forget that the British Museum stole 2000 bronze works from Nigeria's city of Benin, never to be returned!).This is art from the heart whereas so much Western art is, as critic George Steiner said, "more interesting for its THEORY than  for its art." I really think it's very worthwhile seeing this museum for its ART (and not just to be pampered through beautiful galleries as in the US and  Europe).

title: VERY POOR FOR THE LARGEST ECONOMY IN AFRICA
text: Have not experienced such small and run down 'national' museum for almost 25 years ( 1990s in Cambodia ) and this is supposed to be the biggest economy in Africa! Sure one can understand lack of budget / expertise etc but surely there is zero excuse for a large country not to put some money into its culture showcase....

title: A good background of history
text: Not so much collections or artefacts but they have some collections that will amaze you especially when you're new in Nigeria. Compared to other museums in other countries, this place might not so special but you will shed a tear when you read about the scars from their faces.

title: The Museum of Nigerian Arts and Culture
text:
The National Museum in Onikan on the Lagos Island in Nigeria is famous for having some of the legacies of 2000 years of Nigerian Arts and Culture and for the regular Art exhibitions. I curated the 1993 World AIDS Day Art Exhibition at the museum where all the artworks sold out and made me famous!
The museum kitchen restaurant here is more than 30 years old and popular for hosting live musical shows of Highlife, Jazz and modern Nigerian hip hop and drama. The museum also has facilities for weddings and other social events.

title: Could Be Better
text:
I was impressed that the air conditioning worked but the lighting sucked. I could barely see the details in most art pieces there. Our tour guide was more into talking to the caucasian tourists like they were part of slavery/colonialism (and in a funny accent).

The apt name is 'The National Cave'. Lights please!! And invest in procurement, there's barely anything of note left there.

title: Poorly Presented Glory
text: From the outside, a visit looks promising but to say I was disappointed is an understatement. Our glory is a shadow of it self and the environment looks a bit unkept but for the foreigner, a visit might be worth it as they would learn a few things about Nigeria. Just opposite the Muson Centre, It's easily accessible from Awolowo Road, Victoria Island or Lagos Island axis.

title: unfulfilled potential
text: I have been three times - partly in the hope that it would get better and that I might have missed something. For a National museum there are so few exhibits and what exists is badly displayed. It could be so much better if someone 'loved' it a bit. History does not seem important.

title: Take in so much of culture and tradition as you cam
text: The national Muesuem is located in a very exciting part of town. It is right besides the Onikan City mall and opposite the Muson Centre (Musical Society of Nigeria). While you need some two hours or more tho fully explore the musuem, I will advise tourists to plan to spend the whole day in that axis. After you visit to the Museum, you can see a movie at the cinema next door or have a meal in the restaurants next door or in the Muson Centre.

text:

title: Tournage pour DAHOMEY DISCOVERY
text:
"Sur les pas de mes ancêtres..."

Faire cette découverte avec mes enfants a été un moment chargé d’émotion. Marcher sur les terres d’Abomey, ressentir l’histoire, toucher les murs du passé… c’est une expérience inoubliable. Transmettre cela à mes enfants, c’est leur offrir une part de leur héritage, de leur identité. Merci à tous ceux qui œuvrent pour préserver cette mémoire vivante. Je recommande à toutes les familles afro-descendantes de faire ce voyage symbolique au moins une fois dans leur vie.

title: Peu de choses à voir à part le temple vaudou caméléon
text: Une visite relativement réduite. Le palais d’Abomey est en restauration, donc pas de visite, la partie accessible est seulement une grande cour où vous trouverez les échoppes traditionnelles pour touriste. La visite/tour complète est plus interessante de par les explications du guide. On vous emmènera voir différents palais/cases où à part quelques décorations sur les murs vous ne verrez que des bâtiments vides mais cela reste interessant de par les explications. Le point le plus sympa reste le marché des fétiches vaudou (photos payantes en plus) et la basilique vaudou caméléon où l’on peut rentrer en se déchaussant avant. Le monastère vaudou situé à côté ne se visite pas mais sa décoration est sympa. Parlons du prix : tout est négociable. Le guide qui se présentera à vous devant le palais vous accompagnera pour le circuit en négociant un prix global incluant les différents tickets d’entrée (pour quelles entrées, on se demande). Compter 15K CFA pour le tout. Si vous êtes accompagné d’un béninois, vous aurez plus de chance de réduire le prix. La visite nécessite une voiture avec chauffeur pour se déplacer d’un endroit à un autre.

title: Visite assez chère et d’intérêt limité
text:
Le palais est en rénovation. Il n’est pas visitable actuellement. Malgré cela, un employé du service touristique et un guide nous ont proposé de visiter un certain nombre de sites attenants. Après négociations, leurs tarifs se sont montés à 8000 + 10 000 = 18 000 CFA. A cela s’est ajouté la location d’une voiture (indispensable pour une visite), soit 15 000 CFA.

Cette visite d’environ 3 heures a été moyennement intéressante. La plus grande partie du temps a été consommée en déplacements, les distances étant très grandes. A part un site, il était impossible d’entrer à cause des rénovations. Pour cette raison il m’est un peu difficile de juger mais il semble que beaucoup de « palais » sont réduits à un petit édifice. Le guide déconseillait d’en visiter d’autres, notamment celui du roi Behanzin, parce que cela conduirait à des « complications » = offrandes à faire…

Ce guide était excellent et connaissait sur le bout des doigts l’histoire du Bénin et aussi les détails de la religion vaudoun, point fort de la visite avec un passage au village coeur de cette religion, qui comprend un couvent (inaccessible aux non adeptes). J’ai beaucoup appris, mais cela ne contrebalance pas le coût de la visite et l’indigence des choses à voir.

title: Wygląda bardzo kiepsko.
text:
Już od wejścia widać ,że nie jest to obiekt zadbany .Kompleks dwunastu tzw. pałaców królewskich to w rzeczywistości niczym specjalnym nie wyróżniające się parterowe  budynki. text:
A visit to the palace(s) is something you must do. But it is really a pity it is not better maintained. It has great historic and cultural value.

Guide : Hyacinthe  + 229 95 54 46 33

The Palace is still being used by the King, so when the king is there you take off your shoes (hot sand!)  And can be a bit crowded because of ceremonies.

title: Interesting and peaceful place to visit
text:
We really enjoyed our visit but agree with others that there isn’t much information given by the palace itself, so for the best experience you should go with a guide. With a guide we found the visit and the palace really interesting and enjoyed learning about the history of Abomey. 
(We visited with English-speaking guide, Mark, who is one of a group of guides from across the country who were trained up by the government. Mark was excellent and showed us all the best sites of Abomey. We sadly did not note down his surname but your hotel should be able to help you find him, as ours did).

title: Une visite incontournable à Abomey
text: Il n'y a pas grand chose à voir malheureusement car la plupart des bâtiments ne sont pas accessibles. On prend conscience de la taille du site, l'histoire est bien racontée par les guides, mais il est interdit de photographier ( alors que de nos jours ce sont les réseaux sociaux qui suscitent l'envie ). Les quelques reliques sont enfermées dans des présentoirs poussiéreux dans des bâtiments sans éclairage. Vraiment dommage car le Bénin tient là un potentiel touristique exceptionnel qu'il ne sait malheureusement pas exploiter. Cela reste tout de même une visite incontournable à Abomey.

title: Interesting regional history
text:
The tour has to be done without shoes and it's a big compound, We were also told that photos weren't allowed during the tour. Organizing a guide is essential because there is a lot of history and there aren't any plaques through the palace describing the artifacts or functions. It is still a functioning palace and while we were there the acting King was holding court in the main courtyard and there were ceremonies which was interesting to experience. 

It was explained to us that the Kingdom of Abomey was the only kingdom in West Africa with an female security force which was established when one of the queens was ruling the kingdom for some years. Our guide explained this to us but the tour would have been improved if there was a plaque that described the circumstances and historical context. 

There were several interesting displays especially the original thrown which was very tall and was resting on the skulls of defeated kings.

title: Abomey mérite mieux que des palais dégradés !
text:
Abomey a été depuis le premier roi Gangnihesdou ( 1600-1621) jusqu'au dernier Behanzin ( 1889-1894)  un puissant royaume appelé plus tard  royaume du Dahomey ( nom francisé). Ces rois de droit divin et au pouvoir absolu , avaient droit de vie et de mort sur leurs sujets.  Ils pratiquaient la décapitation , sans hésiter.  Ils ont , pendant la période de l'esclavage, vendu nombre de leurs vaincus et de leurs sujets aux négriers européens . Le marché de Ouidah a été florissant pendant des siècles.

Le système royal est entièrement réglé par le roi qui dispose d'un nombre important de concubines qui sont suppervisees par la reine mère.  Les derniers rois utilisaient  des amazones, femmes entraînées à la guerre , qui sont restées fidèles jusqu'à dernier moment pendant la conquête française, qui a déposé le roi Behanzin en 1894 . Avec sa redoutable armée,  le royaume à vassalise les autres royaumes de l'actuel Bénin à l'exception de celui de Hogbonou ( Porto Novo ) où le roi  Joffa avait déjà conclu un accord commercial avec la France en 1882.
Le roi Behanzin , bien qu'ayant règne que 5 ans , est très populaire , car  il est le symbole de la résistance contre l'envahisseur français   qui a eut du mal à le vaincre, malgré une supériorité numérique et technologique. 

La visite de ce musée est décevante  , par la vétusté des lieux , la médiocrité en valeur des quelques objets et par l'interdiction de prendre des photos , que je considère comme contre productive pour la promotion du site .Seules les explications  du guide sont détaillées et intéressantes. Le seul endroit où les photos sont autorisées est la première cour où les marchands du temple présentent leurs objets pour touristes. A noter que ce qui donne une impression de dégradation sont les tôles rouillées qui ont remplacé les toits traditionnels en paille . De même, les vitrines qui présentent des objets sont tellement sales qu 'on a du mal à les distinguer !

L'entrée est payante 1000 francs pour les beninois et 3000 francs pour les autres .

title: Très bel héritage du royaume du Dahomey
text: Vaste domaine royal où l'on peut découvrir le passé culturel très riche de cette partie du Bénin. Très bon guide en prime

title: Une visite incontournable et intéressante
text: Je n'étais plus allé la-bas depuis des années. Malheureusement l'endroit est décrépie faute d'argent pour l'entretenir. C'est désormais gratuit pour tous. Un excellent guide connaissant bien son histoire nous à fait visiter les lieux pendant 1H30. c'était bien expliqué. Pas grand chose à voir dans les bâtiments et les quelques objets exposés sont poussiéreux et les vitrines suffisamment sales pour empêcher de lire les explications. Malgré cela, ça reste intéressant, il faut le faire. Les artisans locaux, à la sortie, sont sympas et les articles pas trop chers ( mais bien sur, toujours négocier le prix ). N'oublier pas de prendre une bouteille d'eau avec vous.

title: See it - but with a guide
text:
Its a little difficult for an European to be impressed by these few clay-based, single story bulidings. They are ancient by the standards in Benin, as they have been constructed around 1830-ish. Unfortunately they did not refurbish ANY of the furniture, maps & graphics hanging on the walls. Most of them are impossible to read. 

They have a much venerated grave of the king Ghezo, which they believe is still with us, as the hut was supposed to be his room. There used to be furniture, but they threw it out, and nobody cared enough to even put a random bed  and some chairs there to pretend that they are the originals. 

There are a few artifacts in the museum - some of them very interesting but in high state of disrepair. By that I mean that they are literally falling apart. The famous  throne with 4 skulls is in a glass cabinet so dirty that you can barely see the shape of that throne.

But dont be discouraged by all this. Get a guide to tell you the stories behind all that and you will really enjoy your time.

title: A must for the history!
text: A rather interesting but harsh history of the royals. I'd definitely recommend as a lot of history here. Guide was excellent. The grounds are v big. Definitely worth a visit..

title: le roi Béhanzin
text:
e #Roi_Gbèhanzin et une partie de sa famille ont été déportés vers la Martinique. Après plusieurs années d'une farouche guerre anticolonialiste, #Gbèhanzin se rendra au Colonel Dodds pour épargner son peuple mais aussi pour essayer d'aller trouver des explications à cette invasion auprès du président français Carnot. 

Le roi du Danxomè se faisait alors accompagner de son fils Wanignilo, de son cousin Adandédjan, 3 de ses filles, 4 reines et du couple Fanou, son traducteur. 

Gbèhanzin ne rencontrera jamais aucun président français, il mourra 12 ans plus tard à Blida (Algérie) de colère et de maladie.

La suite, c'est 125 ans de pillage, d'humiliation, de déshumanisation, qui laisseront place à la corruption, l'irresponsabilité et à l'incurie de notre élite.

title: le roi béhanzin
text:
Béhanzin né en 1845 et mort en 1906, est traditionnellement le onzième roi d’Abomey. Fils de Da-Da Glèlè Kini-Kini, Béhanzin est d’abord connu sous le nom d’Ahokponu puis de prince Kondo à partir de 1875.

Béhanzin est Roi du Dahomey du 6 janvier 1890 au 15 janvier 1894, date de sa reddition. Il décède à Blida (Alger) le 10 décembre 1906. Être sacré, il porte plusieurs titres : Dada (père de toute la communauté), Dokounnon (détenteur et dispensateur de biens), Sèmèdo (maître du monde), Aïnon (maître de la terre), Jèhossou (maître des perles), etc.

Ses insignes de pouvoir sont le kataklè (tabouret tripode), les afokpa (sandales), le avotita (pagne tissé et décoré de motifs appliqués), le awè (parasol), le makpo (spetre), le so (fusil) et lehwi (sabre). Il a été marié à douze femmes et a eu probablement plus de cinquante enfants.

title: Belle héritage du passé.
text: Ce n'est pas le Louvre bien entendu mais une belle part de l'histoire des rois d'Abomey vous sera raconté par des guides compétents. NB, une rénovation du site est prévue, une belle invitation au tourisme au Bénin.

title: Interesting place
text: The place itself does not really look like a palace, but with a good guide you do get the story and the right impression. We liked especially the strange clay figurines on the walls and the stories behind them, they are quite unique. Do ask about their active involvement in the slave trade - it made them insanely rich and powerful.

title: Форт Эльмина
text: Мне очень понравился этот форт, больше чем аналогичный в кейп кост. Был построен еще в 1482 году и служил впоследствии в качестве перевалочной базы для отправки рабов в Америку.

title: Should visit
text:
The Elmina Slave Fort is a castle built by the Portuguese as a Slave holding area before they were shipped to the Americas. Though it reminds one of the horrors humans inflict on humans, it should be visited to ensure such horrors are not repeated. The British won this from the Dutch who had kicked the Portuguese out but all three empires used this outpost for their slave trading activities, till the British Privy Council abolished slavery in England and the British Empire.

It is a three and a half hour drive on a Sunday and a little longer on other days of the week.
One should combine it with a visit to the Cape Coast slave fort which is on the same road, half an hour

title: Elmina castle
text: I’m studying in Cape Coast and visited Elmina Castle. Very informative guide with a lot of knowledge. A really great place to visit to learn about colonialism and slave trade in Ghana and Africa

title: Harrowing experience
text:
Unbelievable suffering for the slaves whom were captured and brutalised here.   Squeezed  in a cell with many others and be faced with  human mental, emotional and physical torture. Never having privacy to conduct normal human daily function and then having to sleep amongst or on it was soul destroying .
One word......Harrowing!!

title: Life changing
text: All I can say is that this was a life changing visit. It was painful to see what the diaspora of West Africans suffered. It stands as a reminder for humanity to be better in the present and future. HIGHLY RECOMMEND!!!

title: Terribly impressive and moving.
text: An exhaustive guided tour through the excruciatingly painful history of the castle : the appalling slaves' confinement rooms leading to the "door of no return".

title: Visit to Elmina with Worlanyo Tours
text: It was an amazing experience, seeing all that with have read and heard about slave trade in Ghana in person, with these castles posing us evidence to that. Our visit to the castle was combined with a visit to the fishing community to meet with the Chief fisherman and his entourage, Fort Jago and the old Dutch colonial cemetery. In all, the experience was tremendous and thank Worlanyo Tours for putting all together.

title: Amazing
text:
Our visit to Elmina castle was a great but sombre experience. Our tour guide Ato was exceptional and extremely knowledgable. I learned so much. I plan on visiting again the next time I’m in Ghana. You simply can’t miss out in this opportunity.
To actually stand in a part of my history was such a special moment. To see the conditions they endured, to stand in the exact place where people died, were chained, the door of no return...I simply can’t forget.
Do yourself a favour and visit.

title: Sorrowful Memories That Never Disappears.
text:
Elmina Castle which is also known as St. George Castle is recognized by UNSESCO as a World Heritage Site. Elmina Castle, erected by the Portuguese in 1482, was the first trading post built on the Gulf of Guinea, and the castle is the oldest European building in existence in the Sahara. Pay a visit to the Castle as well as the fishing harbour and market. If you like, walk up the hill to visit 	Fort St Jago, offering wonderful panoramic views over the town.
As a tour guide working in Ghana, if you ask me, i will say, yes, Elmina Castle is the oldest castle having rich history on the slave trade but to have a real experience regarding the slave trade, you need to be at the Cape Coast Castle where the castle itself tells the story of what actually happened there regarding the slave trade,
a. The palaver hall where the slaves were sold and branded is bigger.
b. The male dungeon which connect through a tunnel to the female dungeon and leading to the sea where boats wait to take the slaves to a land unknown to them against their will. The dungeon at the Cape Coast castle held hundreds or thousands at a time.
c. The door of no return which is now known as a door of return is well structured for the human cargo to pass swiftly without much efforts into the waiting ships which carries the slaves away forever.

title: A story worth knowing
text:
Compared to the cape coast castle, I honestly really liked the elmina castle more.

A lot more to see, a better picture of the past was painted verbally with physical evidence

Hard to photograph as everything is huge and close.

Entry fee 5gh (locals) 40gh (foreign) comes with a tour guide. Tours are mostly conducted in groups

An emotional tour for some but definitely thought provoking and conversation starter for all.

Guides welcome questions and try their best to answer

Regards

title: Beautiful castle, with deep signifigance
text:
Elmina is the largest slave castle in the world. We had a wonderful tour guide that explained things so perfectly to our kids. We learned that once the slaves set foot in the castle, they could spend up to three months in horrific conditions. And that “The door of no return” was a portal through which the slaves were lowered into small boats and then loaded onto bigger ships further out to sea, never to set foot in their homeland again and with a final goodbye to the freedom they once knew.  Our kids are young, but were able to follow the guides teachings.
Only down side was the hawkers in the parking lot.  Very pushy, but not a reason not to go.  Just be prepared to say no if you are not interested.

title: Must see when in Ghana
text:
Elmina Castle is a must see when in Ghana to better understand the history of the county and horrors that happend here.

Our tour guide was really good. Telling the facts as they are, but not blaming anybody. I am Dutch and my people played a major roll in Elminas history. I did not felt blamed, but humbled to walk together with a Ghanaian friend in Elmina. A very intense place. A place we need to preserve and protect. Something they are doing very well!

title: Great attraction aside from the beggars
text:
This really is a must see attraction and a World Heritage site. Our guide was fantastic, tailoring our tour to suit the ages of the children in our group, aged 9 to 15.  It is a most excellent insight into the history of the castle, and what those poor people went through. 

I wish that some investment came with being a World Heritage site. It is a great place as it is, but you can see how it might be improved with just a little more funding. 

The only downside was the hassle we received from the people outside the castle. I’ve been traveling to Ghana regularly for 20 years and this was definitely the worst I’ve experienced. 

They seemed friendly at first, asking for our names. But there was a catch - they’d put our names onto shells (without asking) when we came out of the castle and asked for payment for having done this. When this wasn’t successful they wanted us to put our names and contact information on a piece of paper - which we didn’t do. They said it was to sponsor their football team which, of course, is fictional. They were overly persistent, even when told that we already support a football team and school in Ghana.  When this didn’t work they resorted to just asking for money. 

Anyway, don’t be put off from visiting. Just be aware that these people hang around and that these are their tricks!

title: Interessante geschiedenis
text: Het kasteel zelf is heel indrukwekkend en zeker de moeite om te bezoeken. De geschiedenis erachter is erg interessant. De gids had er geen zin in en hield alles heel kort, mompelde meestal onverstaanbaar en reageerde kwaad als we een vraag stelden.

title: Historia de esclavitud
text: Fuerte de tiempos coloniales, donde se controlaba la costa y donde se negociaba con los esclavos. Merece la pena la visita

title: A harrowing insight into the shame of the past.
text:
This cannot be described as an enjoyable day out by any means, it is a stark and harrowing place to be, and shows just what barbarians the human race can produce. 

The guide we had was very knowledgable, and posed searching questions as well as explaining the history of the whole disgraceful time of slavery. His words around the last govenor of the prison, and the poem written about him as a "god fearing, honorable man" were resonant - simply to say that in a time of slavery, how this man was god fearing and honourable was, perhaps, something that only he could explain.

There are alot of people who could do with a visit here when they spout off about immigration, and their far right political views - this is exactly the sort of thing that could possibly put right some of the wrongs that still plague proportions of the western population.

It was a deeply moving experience, and while it isn't nice, if you're here you need to see it - in the same way as you need to see the holocaust experience. As uncomfortable as it is for a western white person, we need to cement in our minds that these appalling things must never happen again, and that the modern equivalents of the people who did this, and are trying to promote inequality (read Nigel Farage etc.) must be prevented from having a platform to try and return to this type of inhumane treatment and abuse.

It's a piece of history that everybody should understand and regret.

title: Beauty and horror
text: The castle is huge and you go on a guided tour. There are occasional stops at small shops within the castle. You see the beautiful scenery of the ocean views and you duck under the small doorways that people sold into slavery were trapped in. It's an important place to visit. Bring toilet paper and a camera. You will stay at least an hour.

title: Elmina Castle - a haunting but unforgettable experience
text:
Elmina Castle in Ghana's Cape Coast region was built as a fort by the Portuguese in 1482, and is the oldest building in sub-Saharan Africa.

Now a World Heritage Site, the Portuguese and then Dutch imprisoned hundreds of thousands of slaves before they were shipped to the Americas. It's a haunting, sad place, and a reminder how cruel humans can be to one another. Slaves were imprisoned in the harshest conditions, and many died here. Slaves that attempted to rebellion were thrown in a dungeon that was only opened when the last had died.

Ironically, there's a church in the centre of the castle.

In the room where hundreds of women were kept, there is still an acrid smell, hundreds of years after the last slaves were here. 

You can hire a driver for $100 to $150 for the day in Accra, to take you to Elmina and the nearby Kakum National Park, where there's an amazing canopy tour. You'll pay about 40 Ghanaian Cedis for a 1-1.5 hour tour of the castle. 

Wear comfortable walking shoes.

title: Wow. Do not miss this!
text: This UNESCO World Heritage Site is a must-see for your visit to Ghana. 550 year old castle that for several hundred years held 1,000 slaves at a time chained in dungeons before they were loaded onto ships bound for North America and the Caribbean. The guided tour is excellent. Nice gift shop.

title: Moving Experience
text: Elmina castle was one of the largest castles used to camp slaves during the Trans-Atlantic slave trade era. Our tour guide took us to some of the dungeons where the slaves were kept and to the tiny exit each slave went through to the ships when they arrived. A visit here will help you to appreciate the suffering humanity endured during that era and hope that it never occurs again.

title: Don’t miss! Arrange a guide to get the full benefit.
text:
We had a local fellow named Ali who was magnificent, taking us through and giving us information on each room and how the slaves would arrive and be treated throughout their time here. You don’t want to miss understanding the impact of this place in history. 
If you really want to understand the impact of the place, make sure you have a guided tour.

title: Edifiant
text:
Visite très intéressante et émouvante, très instructive. A conseiller aux ados (et pas seulement)...
De plus, l’île de Gorée a un charme fou, ce qui permet de ne pas rester sur une note trop triste.

text: prenez un guide pour visiter l'île, vous ne serez pas embeté constamment par les vendeuses de petites boutiques. la visite vaut le coup, meme si tout est en tres mauvais état. Le musée dans le fort n'a aucun interet et tout est poussiereux.

text:

title: La maison des esclaves
text: C'est un endroit qui ma marqué dans m'a vie.En le visitant j'ai même pleuré en étant au courant de l'énorme souffrance de nos anceitres.C'est un lieu que j'invite a toutes les africains a visité.

title: We are not "free"
text: The "door of no return". My emotions ran deep as I stood in the door where my ancestors boarded ships to destinations unknown. Some of the girls were not able to finish the tour when a group of Europeans came through. The tour is run by locals, but they told us to end our tour so they could be accomodated. Our curator clearly put on a dog and pony show to entertain us. My people are still brainwashed. I paid the same price as them and should have the same amount of time to explore. This left us all very upset and disappointed!

title: Sad Ending to the Experience
text: Our tour group of black American women arrived early for a private tour. The curator explained the history of the house and the planned restoration. Everyone was very moved. Then a group white tourist showed up and they began to rush us out. As the sisters took photos of the door our ancestors were herded through the white French visitors began to complain loudly about waiting in line, apparently anxious enjoy their colonizing memories. Sadly the curator chose his masters once again.

title: Incontournable
text:
Passage obligatoire si vous êtes de passage sur l’île de Gorée. 
Tout y est très bien expliqué par le guide présent pour un prix plus que raisonnable !

title: En restauration
text:
Maison en pleins travaux, installation de l'éclairage dans les cellules. J'ai peur que cela altère l'authenticité des lieux.

Le Sénégal devrait peut-être demander au très beau musée de l'esclavage a la Guadeloupe de lui prêter quelques pièces de sa collection afin d'agrémenter ces lieux ici relativement vides pour le moment.

la maison des esclaves charge en histoire on ce rappelle cette peroide funeste tel que la shoa aussi
